claim: C. elegans egg laying alternates between inactive and active states.
source: Like many behaviors, Caenorhabditis elegans egg laying alternates between inactive and active states.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a fundamental characteristic of the behavior being studied.

claim: In the active state, the egg-laying circuit shows rhythmic activity phased with the body bends of locomotion.
source: In the active state, the circuit shows rhythmic activity phased with the body bends of locomotion.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The serotonergic HSN command neurons initiate the active state.
source: The serotonergic HSN command neurons initiate the active state, but accumulation of unlaid eggs also promotes the active state independent of the HSNs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by optogenetic experiments in Figure 3.

claim: Accumulation of unlaid eggs promotes the active state independent of the HSNs.
source: The serotonergic HSN command neurons initiate the active state, but accumulation of unlaid eggs also promotes the active state independent of the HSNs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experiments with egl-1(dm) mutants lacking HSNs in Figure 4.

claim: The cholinergic VC motor neurons slow locomotion during egg-laying muscle contraction and egg release.
source: The cholinergic VC motor neurons slow locomotion during egg-laying muscle contraction and egg release.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3C showing reduced locomotion speed during egg release.

claim: The uv1 neuroendocrine cells mechanically sense passage of eggs through the vulva.
source: The uv1 neuroendocrine cells mechanically sense passage of eggs through the vulva and release tyramine to inhibit egg laying, in part via the LGC-55 tyramine-gated Cl- channel on the HSNs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by Ca2+ imaging data in Figure 5 showing uv1 activation during egg passage.

claim: The uv1 cells release tyramine to inhibit egg laying.
source: The uv1 neuroendocrine cells mechanically sense passage of eggs through the vulva and release tyramine to inhibit egg laying, in part via the LGC-55 tyramine-gated Cl- channel on the HSNs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by tyramine behavior assays and genetic experiments in Figure 6.

claim: Tyramine inhibits egg laying in part via the LGC-55 tyramine-gated Cl- channel on the HSNs.
source: The uv1 neuroendocrine cells mechanically sense passage of eggs through the vulva and release tyramine to inhibit egg laying, in part via the LGC-55 tyramine-gated Cl- channel on the HSNs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experiments showing lgc-55 mutants are resistant to tyramine inhibition and have increased HSN activity in Figure 6.

claim: The egg-laying circuit consists of two serotonergic Hermaphrodite Specific Neurons (HSNs) and six cholinergic Ventral C neurons (VCs), each of which synapse onto a set of vulval muscles whose contraction expels eggs.
source: This circuit, diagrammed in Figure 1A, consists of two serotonergic Hermaphrodite Specific Neurons (HSNs) and six cholinergic Ventral C neurons (VCs), each of which synapse onto a set of vulval muscles whose contraction expels eggs.
evidence: This is a description of the circuit anatomy based on established knowledge and cited in the introduction.

claim: Four neuroendocrine uv1 cells regulate egg laying.
source: Four neuroendocrine uv1 cells also regulate egg laying (Jose et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work.

claim: The egg-laying behavior alternates between quiescent periods of about 20 min during which no egg laying occurs, and active states lasting a few minutes during which ~5 eggs are laid.
source: Despite its anatomical simplicity, the egg-laying circuit produces a regulated, rhythmic behavior that alternates between quiescent periods of about 20 min during which no egg laying occurs, and active states lasting a few minutes during which ~5 eggs are laid (Waggoner et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to previous work.

claim: Active states appear to result when the HSNs release serotonin that signals through G protein coupled receptors on the vulval muscles to increase their excitability.
source: Active states appear to result when the HSNs release serotonin that signals through G protein coupled receptors on the vulval muscles to increase their excitability (Waggoner et al., 1998; Shyn et al., 2003; Hapiak et al., 2009; Emtage et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to previous work.

claim: HSN transients were more frequent during the active state compared to the inactive state.
source: There was also significant HSN activity outside of the active state, but HSN transients were more frequent during the active state (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantitative data in Figure 1G.

claim: Active state HSN transients typically occurred in bursts, within which HSN transients occurred every ~20 s.
source: Active state HSN transients typically occurred in bursts, within which HSN transients occurred every ~20 s (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 1G.

claim: Only 11% of HSN transients were accompanied by an egg release.
source: Only 11% of HSN transients were accompanied by an egg release (Figure 1H), but almost every egg-laying event occurred during an HSN transient (Figure 1F; out of 49 total egg-laying events observed, 48 occurred within an HSN transient).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantitative data in Figure 1H.

claim: Almost every egg-laying event occurred during an HSN transient (48 out of 49 total egg-laying events).
source: Only 11% of HSN transients were accompanied by an egg release (Figure 1H), but almost every egg-laying event occurred during an HSN transient (Figure 1F; out of 49 total egg-laying events observed, 48 occurred within an HSN transient).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 1F.

claim: VC transients were shorter than HSN transients (~2 s at half-max).
source: VC transients were shorter than HSN transients (~2 s at half-max) and variable in amplitude.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on Ca2+ imaging data.

claim: VC transients were rarely observed during the inactive state, but there was a clear induction of transients during the active state.
source: We rarely observed VC transients during the inactive state, but we found a clear induction of transients during the active state (Video 2; Figure 1F,G), and these transients occurred in bursts around egg-laying events with an inter-transient interval of ~10 s, about twice as frequent as seen for the HSNs.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 1F,G.

claim: VC transients occurred in bursts around egg-laying events with an inter-transient interval of ~10 s, about twice as frequent as seen for the HSNs.
source: We rarely observed VC transients during the inactive state, but we found a clear induction of transients during the active state (Video 2; Figure 1F,G), and these transients occurred in bursts around egg-laying events with an inter-transient interval of ~10 s, about twice as frequent as seen for the HSNs.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 1F,G.

claim: 34% of VC transients were accompanied by an egg release, a larger fraction than seen for HSN and vulval muscle Ca2+ transients.
source: 34% of VC transients were accompanied by an egg release, a larger fraction than seen for HSN and vulval muscle Ca2+ transients (p<0.0001; Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantitative data in Figure 1H.

claim: Every egg-release event was accompanied by a VC transient.
source: Every egg-release event was accompanied by a VC transient.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on Ca2+ imaging observations.

claim: There was no correlation between the magnitudes of VC or HSN transients that did or did not coincide with egg release.
source: There was no correlation seen between the magnitudes of VC or HSN transients that did or did not coincide with egg release, while the magnitude of muscle Ca2+ transients that resulted in egg laying were ~four fold larger than the muscle twitch transients that did not release eggs (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 1H.

claim: The magnitude of muscle Ca2+ transients that resulted in egg laying were ~four fold larger than the muscle twitch transients that did not release eggs.
source: There was no correlation seen between the magnitudes of VC or HSN transients that did or did not coincide with egg release, while the magnitude of muscle Ca2+ transients that resulted in egg laying were ~four fold larger than the muscle twitch transients that did not release eggs (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 1H.

claim: HSN Ca2+ transients peaked ~2 s prior to egg release.
source: HSN Ca2+ transients peaked ~2 s prior to egg release (Figure 1I) and decayed slowly.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 1I.

claim: VC Ca2+ transients peaked ~0.1 s before egg release.
source: Shorter VC Ca2+ transients followed HSN activity, peaking ~0.1 s before egg release.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 1I.

claim: Vulval muscle Ca2+ transients peaked with egg laying.
source: Vulval muscle Ca2+ transients peaked with egg laying.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 1I.

claim: Muscle relaxation and decay of vulval muscle Ca2+ immediately followed egg release.
source: We also tracked vulval muscle contraction by measuring the size and fluorescence intensity of the mCherry labeled muscles, and saw that muscle relaxation and decay of vulval muscle Ca2+ immediately followed egg release (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 1I.

claim: Timing of egg-laying events was not rhythmic but followed a Poisson distribution.
source: Previous work showed that timing of egg-laying events was not rhythmic but followed a Poisson distribution (Waggoner et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to previous work.

claim: HSN, VC, and vulval muscles showed rhythmic activity during the egg-laying active state.
source: However, we found that HSN, VC, and vulval muscles showed rhythmic activity during the egg-laying active state.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by power spectrum analysis in Figure 2.

claim: Rhythms in HSN and VC were similar, peaking at ~50 mHz with smaller peaks observed at ~100 and ~140 mHz.
source: Rhythms in HSN and VC were similar, peaking at ~50 mHz with smaller peaks observed at ~100 and~140 mHz (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by power spectrum data in Figure 2B and C.

claim: The 50 mHz rhythm was clearly evident in the vulval muscles, but the 100 mHz peak was significantly stronger.
source: The 50 mHz rhythm was also clearly evident in the vulval muscles (Figure 2D), but the 100 mHz peak was significantly stronger (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by power spectrum data in Figure 2D and E.

claim: HSN, VC, and vulval muscle Ca2+ transients occurred when the vulva was at particular phases of the locomotor body bend.
source: We found that the HSN, VC, and vulval muscle Ca2+ transients occurred when the vulva was at particular phases of the locomotor body bend.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by phasing analysis in Figure 2G-I.

claim: HSN transients just prior to egg release reached their maximum at ~180°, when the vulva and adjacent body wall muscles were at their most relaxed state.
source: HSN transients just prior to egg release reached their maximum at ~180°, when the vulva and adjacent body wall muscles were at their most relaxed state (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by phasing data in Figure 2G.

claim: VC and vulval muscle transients that accompanied egg laying occurred at ~225°.
source: VC and vulval muscle transients that accompanied egg laying occurred later, starting at ~225° (Figure 2H and I).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by phasing data in Figure 2H and I.

claim: HSN transients that did not result in egg laying showed no clear evidence of phasing.
source: HSN transients that did not result in egg laying showed no clear evidence of phasing (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by phasing data in Figure 2G.

claim: VC transients and vulval muscle twitch transients that did not lead to egg release were still phased, but delayed by ~45° toward the most ventral contracted state.
source: In contrast, VC transients and vulval muscle twitch transients that did not lead to egg release were still phased, but delayed by ~45° toward the most ventral contracted state.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by phasing data in Figure 2H and I.

claim: Optogenetic activation of HSNs stimulates egg-laying behavior.
source: We repeated the observation of Emtage et al. (2012) that optogenetic activation of HSNs stimulates egg-laying behavior (Video 4), but we activated the HSNs while simultaneously recording behavior and Ca2+ activity in the VCs (Figure 3A) or vulval muscles (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to previous work and supported by new data in Figure 3.

claim: Activation of HSNs resulted in circuit activity reminiscent of a spontaneous active state, including rhythmic Ca2+ activity of both VCs and vulval muscles, and egg-laying events that accompanied a subset of these Ca2+ transients.
source: We found that activation of HSNs resulted in circuit activity reminiscent of a spontaneous active state, including rhythmic Ca2+ activity of both VCs and vulval muscles, and egg-laying events that accompanied a subset of these Ca2+ transients.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The high level of HSN activity after optogenetic activation induces strong coupling of VC and vulval muscle excitation.
source: These results suggest that the high level of HSN activity after optogenetic activation induces strong coupling of VC and vulval muscle excitation.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the results based on the observation that optogenetic HSN activation leads to more frequent egg-laying events.

claim: The most dramatic Ca2+ changes during vulval muscle twitching occur at the ventral tips of the vm1 muscles.
source: Careful observation shows that the most dramatic Ca2+ changes during vulval muscle twitching occur at the ventral tips of the vm1 muscles (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on Ca2+ imaging observations.

claim: The VCs innervate vm2 muscles but not the vm1 muscles.
source: The VCs innervate vm2 muscles but not the vm1 muscles.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on anatomical knowledge.

claim: The vm1 muscles are innervated by the VB6 and VA7 neurons that also release acetylcholine to drive body wall muscle contraction for locomotion.
source: The vm1 muscles are instead innervated by the VB6 and VA7 neurons that also release acetylcholine to drive body wall muscle contraction for locomotion (White et al., 1986).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to previous anatomical work.

claim: vm1 twitching occurs at the same time the adjacent ventral body wall muscles are contracting during locomotion.
source: Consistent with this, vm1 twitching occurs at the same time the adjacent ventral body wall muscles are contracting during locomotion (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by phasing data in Figure 2.

claim: Increased electrical excitability of the vulval muscles during a spontaneous or optogenetically-induced active state may allow for vm1 excitation by VB6/VA7 with each body bend.
source: Increased electrical excitability of the vulval muscles during a spontaneous or optogenetically-induced active state may allow for vm1 excitation by VB6/VA7 with each body bend.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism stated in the results based on the observations.

claim: VC activity always accompanies egg release.
source: Our observation that VC activity always accompanies egg release (Figures 1I and 3A) is consistent with a proposal that the VCs release acetylcholine that signals through vulval muscle nicotinic receptors to drive egg laying (Waggoner et al., 2000; Kim et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figures 1I and 3A.

claim: There was a clear and significant reduction of locomotion speed beginning ~1 s before egg release, a time when VC activity is increasing.
source: We found a clear and significant reduction of locomotion speed beginning ~1 s before egg release, a time when VC activity is increasing (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: Locomotion speed recovered immediately after egg release.
source: Locomotion speed recovered immediately after egg release (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: Acetylcholine released from the VCs slows locomotion during egg laying.
source: These results are consistent with the hypothesis that acetylcholine released from the VCs slows locomotion during egg laying.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the results based on the observation of slowed locomotion during egg release.

claim: Optogenetic activation of the VC neurons was not sufficient to drive egg laying.
source: Optogenetic activation of the VCs was not sufficient to drive egg laying (Figure 3F), but did lead to a rapid shortening of the body (Video 5 and Figure 3D) and cessation of locomotion (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 3F.

claim: Optogenetic activation of the VC neurons led to a rapid shortening of the body and cessation of locomotion.
source: Optogenetic activation of the VCs was not sufficient to drive egg laying (Figure 3F), but did lead to a rapid shortening of the body (Video 5 and Figure 3D) and cessation of locomotion (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 3D and E.

claim: The shortening phenotype seen in VC ChR2 animals after blue light exposure closely resembles that seen for optogenetic activation of the body wall muscles.
source: The shortening phenotype seen in VC ChR2 animals after blue light exposure closely resembles that seen for optogenetic activation of the body wall muscles (Nagel et al., 2005), except the head and tail of VC-activated animals were still mobile and active, consistent with the fact that VC neurons innervate only the central body wall muscles (White et al., 1976).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to previous work.

claim: While VC activity immediately precedes egg-laying events, it is not sufficient to drive egg release.
source: Our results indicate that while VC activity immediately precedes egg-laying events, it is not sufficient to drive egg release.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on optogenetic experiments.

claim: Optogenetic VC activation is sufficient to produce a slowing of locomotion as seen during egg-laying events.
source: Optogenetic VC activation is sufficient to produce a slowing of locomotion as seen during egg-laying events.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: HSN activity is sufficient to induce all of the hallmarks of the active state, including rhythmic vulval muscle twitching, VC transients, and the coordinated vulval muscle contractions that produce egg-laying events.
source: In contrast, HSN activity is sufficient to induce all of the hallmarks of the active state, including rhythmic vulval muscle twitching, VC transients, and the coordinated vulval muscle contractions that produce egg-laying events.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by optogenetic data in Figure 3.

claim: Animals lacking HSNs have a substantial lengthening of the inactive state.
source: Animals lacking HSNs have a substantial lengthening of the inactive state (Waggoner et al., 1998) and are strongly egg-laying defective, accumulating ~50 eggs in the uterus rather than the 12–15 seen in the wild type (Trent et al., 1983).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to previous work.

claim: Animals lacking HSNs are strongly egg-laying defective, accumulating ~50 eggs in the uterus rather than the 12–15 seen in the wild type.
source: Animals lacking HSNs have a substantial lengthening of the inactive state (Waggoner et al., 1998) and are strongly egg-laying defective, accumulating ~50 eggs in the uterus rather than the 12–15 seen in the wild type (Trent et al., 1983).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to previous work.

claim: Animals lacking HSNs had more frequent vulval muscle Ca2+ transients during the inactive state and robust activity during infrequent active states that led to multiple eggs being laid in a short period.
source: Surprisingly, we found the opposite; animals lacking HSNs had more frequent vulval muscle Ca2+ transients during the inactive state and robust activity during infrequent active states that led to multiple eggs being laid in a short period (compare Figure 4A and B; quantitation in Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: There was a significant reduction in the amplitude of vulval muscle Ca2+ transients during egg laying in egl-1(dm) mutants while the amplitude of twitch Ca2+ transients was unaffected.
source: There was a significant reduction in the amplitude of vulval muscle Ca2+ transients during egg laying in egl-1(dm) mutants while the amplitude of twitch Ca2+ transients was unaffected (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 4D.

claim: Vulval muscle activity in egl-1(dm) mutants lacking HSNs resembled the frequent yet uncoordinated vulval muscle activity found in animals missing the vm2 vulval muscle arms onto which the HSNs normally make synapses.
source: Vulval muscle activity in egl-1(dm) mutants lacking HSNs resembled the frequent yet uncoordinated vulval muscle activity found in animals missing the vm2 vulval muscle arms onto which the HSNs normally make synapses (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to previous work.

claim: Overall vulval muscle Ca2+ transient peaks in egl-1(dm) mutants were longer in duration, likely resulting in individual muscle cells beginning their transients at different times.
source: One quantitative measure of this asynchrony is that overall vulval muscle Ca2+ transient peaks in egl-1(dm) mutants were longer in duration, likely resulting in individual muscle cells beginning their transients at different times (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 4E.

claim: Vulval muscle Ca2+ transients in animals lacking HSNs remained phased with locomotion, including the ~45° advance in phase of vulval muscle activity that results in egg-laying events.
source: Vulval muscle Ca2+ transients in animals lacking HSNs remained phased with locomotion, including the ~45° advance in phase of vulval muscle activity that results in egg-laying events (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The HSNs are necessary to coordinate contraction of anterior and posterior vulval muscles.
source: These results suggest that the HSNs are necessary to coordinate contraction of anterior and posterior vulval muscles, and that signals from other cells besides the HSNs can also induce the egg-laying active state.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on observations in egl-1(dm) mutants.

claim: Signals from other cells besides the HSNs can also induce the egg-laying active state.
source: These results suggest that the HSNs are necessary to coordinate contraction of anterior and posterior vulval muscles, and that signals from other cells besides the HSNs can also induce the egg-laying active state.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on observations that egl-1(dm) mutants still enter active states.

claim: FUDR-treated animals had a dramatic reduction of vulval muscle activity and appeared to be stuck in the inactive state, with no egg-laying transients observed.
source: FUDR-treated animals had a dramatic reduction of vulval muscle activity and appeared to be stuck in the inactive state, with no egg-laying transients observed (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The inhibition of vulval muscle activity by FUDR occurred in both wild-type animals and HSN-deficient egl-1(dm) mutants.
source: The inhibition of vulval muscle activity by FUDR occurred in both wild-type animals and HSN-deficient egl-1(dm) mutants (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The residual vulval muscle Ca2+ twitch transients in FUDR-treated animals had phasing identical to those seen in the inactive state of untreated animals.
source: The residual vulval muscle Ca2+ twitch transients in FUDR-treated animals had phasing identical to those seen in the inactive state of untreated animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Germ line activity and/or the accumulation of eggs in the uterus is required to initiate the egg-laying active state.
source: These results suggest that germ line activity and/or the accumulation of eggs in the uterus is required to initiate the egg-laying active state.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on FUDR experiments.

claim: The four uv1 cells sit at the junction between the uterine lumen and the vulval canal.
source: The four uv1 cells sit at the junction between the uterine lumen and the vulval canal (Newman and Sternberg, 1996), and as such are positioned to mechanically sense the accumulation of unlaid eggs in the uterus and/or passage of eggs through the vulval canal as they are laid.
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to previous anatomical work.

claim: The uv1 cells were mechanically deformed as each egg passed through the vulva, and then showed strong Ca2+ transients after egg release.
source: We found that the uv1 cells were mechanically deformed as each egg passed through the vulva, and then showed strong Ca2+ transients after egg release (Figure 5A–B; Video 6).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Ca2+ imaging data in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Egg-laying events did not always trigger Ca2+ transients in uv1, with uv1-silent events usually being the first or last within an active state.
source: Egg-laying events did not always trigger Ca2+ transients in uv1, with uv1-silent events usually being the first or last within an active state (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on observations.

claim: Typical active state uv1 Ca2+ transients began immediately with or slightly before egg release, coinciding with the initial mechanical deformation of uv1 caused by the egg, with the Ca2+ transient peak occurring ~2 s later.
source: Typical active state uv1 Ca2+ transients began immediately with or slightly before egg release, coinciding with the initial mechanical deformation of uv1 caused by the egg, with the Ca2+ transient peak occurring ~2 s later (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 5E.

claim: The uv1 cells are mechanically activated by eggs passing through the vulva during egg laying.
source: Based on the position of the uv1 cells, their morphological deformations during passage of eggs, and the timing of uv1 Ca2+ transients, our data suggest the uv1 cells are mechanically activated by eggs passing through the vulva during egg laying.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on observations of uv1 deformation and Ca2+ activity.

claim: The uv1 cells make the biogenic amine neurotransmitter tyramine.
source: The uv1 cells make the biogenic amine neurotransmitter tyramine, and tdc-1 mutations that disrupt tyramine biosynthesis lead to increased egg-laying behaviors (Alkema et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to previous work.

claim: tdc-1 mutations that disrupt tyramine biosynthesis lead to increased egg-laying behaviors.
source: The uv1 cells make the biogenic amine neurotransmitter tyramine, and tdc-1 mutations that disrupt tyramine biosynthesis lead to increased egg-laying behaviors (Alkema et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to previous work.

claim: Exogenous tyramine reduced egg laying in wild-type animals.
source: We found that exogenous tyramine reduced egg laying in wild-type animals (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 6A.

claim: Animals lacking lgc-55 showed resistance to inhibition by exogenous tyramine.
source: Animals lacking lgc-55, which encodes a tyramine-gated Cl- channel, showed resistance to inhibition by exogenous tyramine (Figure 6A), although tyramine at high levels still had a residual ability to reduce egg laying in lgc-55 mutants (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 6A.

claim: Tyramine at high levels still had a residual ability to reduce egg laying in lgc-55 mutants.
source: Animals lacking lgc-55, which encodes a tyramine-gated Cl- channel, showed resistance to inhibition by exogenous tyramine (Figure 6A), although tyramine at high levels still had a residual ability to reduce egg laying in lgc-55 mutants (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 6B.

claim: LGC-55 is expressed in the HSNs, uv1, and vulval muscles.
source: We transformed into C. elegans a fosmid transgene containing the full-length lgc-55 gene fused to GFP coding sequences, and found LGC-55 is expressed in the HSNs, uv1, and vulval muscles (Figure 6C and Pirri et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by imaging data in Figure 6C and citation to previous work.

claim: Re-expression of LGC-55 specifically in HSN from the tph-1 promoter restored tyramine sensitivity to lgc-55 mutants.
source: Re-expression of LGC-55 specifically in HSN from the tph-1 promoter restored tyramine sensitivity to lgc-55 mutants (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 6D.

claim: Two Cl- extruding transporters, KCC-2 and ABTS-1, are expressed in the HSNs where they promote the development of inhibitory ligand-gated Cl- channel signaling.
source: We have previously shown that two Cl- extruding transporters, KCC-2 and ABTS-1, are expressed in the HSNs where they promote the development of inhibitory ligand-gated Cl- channel signaling (Tanis et al., 2009; Bellemer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to previous work.

claim: Tyramine signaling through LGC-55 would hyperpolarize the HSN and inhibit activity.
source: These data suggest that tyramine signaling through LGC-55 would hyperpolarize the HSN and inhibit activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the expression of LGC-55 and Cl- transporters in HSN.

claim: There was a significant increase in the frequency of Ca2+ transients in HSNs of lgc-55 mutant animals in both the inactive and active states of egg-laying behavior.
source: We observed a significant increase in the frequency of Ca2+ transients in HSNs of lgc-55 mutant animals (Figure 6E and F) in both the inactive and active states of egg-laying behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 6E and F.

claim: Mean HSN inter-transient intervals in wild-type animals were 41 ± 5 s in the inactive state and 17 ± 2 s during the active state.
source: Mean HSN inter-transient intervals in wild-type animals were 41 ± 5 s in the inactive state and 17 ± 2 s during the active state, while intervals in lgc-55 mutants were reduced to 22 ± 2 s in the inactive state and 13 ± 1 s during the active state.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on quantitative analysis of Ca2+ imaging data.

claim: HSN inter-transient intervals in lgc-55 mutants were reduced to 22 ± 2 s in the inactive state and 13 ± 1 s during the active state.
source: Mean HSN inter-transient intervals in wild-type animals were 41 ± 5 s in the inactive state and 17 ± 2 s during the active state, while intervals in lgc-55 mutants were reduced to 22 ± 2 s in the inactive state and 13 ± 1 s during the active state.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on quantitative analysis of Ca2+ imaging data.

claim: The absence of inhibitory feedback by tyramine signaling onto the HSNs leads to increased activity in both the active and inactive egg-laying behavior states.
source: Thus, the absence of inhibitory feedback by tyramine signaling onto the HSNs leads to increased activity in both the active and inactive egg-laying behavior states.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on observations in lgc-55 mutants.

claim: Active state vulval muscle Ca2+ transients peak rhythmically each time the vulva approaches a ventral body bend, the point at which the cholinergic VB and VA motor neurons release acetylcholine to rhythmically excite both the vm1 muscles and adjacent ventral body wall muscles during locomotion.

claim: During the inactive state, K+ channels including ERG depress vulval muscle excitability below threshold.
source: During the inactive state, K+ channels including ERG depress vulval muscle excitability below threshold, explaining why we fail to observe vulval muscle activity with each body bend during this state (Collins and Koelle, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to previous work.

claim: HSN rhythmic activity is independent of locomotion.
source: Thus HSN rhythmic activity is independent of locomotion, although we found HSN Ca2+ transients that happen to fall at a specific phase of locomotor body bends are more likely to be followed by egg release.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on observations that HSN activity does not correlate with locomotion periodicity.

claim: HSN Ca2+ transients that happen to fall at a specific phase of locomotor body bends are more likely to be followed by egg release.

claim: Release of serotonin from the HSNs, along with an unknown signal resulting from mechanical stretch of the uterus by accumulating eggs, together raise vulval muscle electrical excitability to result in the active state.
source: We propose that release of serotonin from the HSNs, along with an unknown signal resulting from mechanical stretch of the uterus by accumulating eggs, together raise vulval muscle electrical excitability to result in the active state during which the vulval muscles undergo rhythmic twitching or egg laying contractions in response to the same cholinergic VA and VB neurons that drive locomotor body bends.
evidence: This is a proposed model stated in the discussion.

claim: vm transients that lead to egg release are on average slightly phase advanced relative to those that do not.
source: We found that vm transients that lead to egg release are on average slightly phase advanced relative to those that do not.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on phasing analysis.

claim: This phase advance could result from the excitatory input onto the vm2 muscles occurring earlier in the body bend, and candidates for this input are the HSNs and VCs, both of which synapse onto the vm2 muscles and have phased activity during egg-laying events.
source: This phase advance could from the excitatory input onto the vm2 muscles occurring earlier in the body bend, and candidates for this input are the HSNs and VCs, both of which synapse onto the vm2 muscles and have phased activity during egg-laying events.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation stated in the discussion.

claim: The functional purpose of the phase advance may be mechanical, as there may not be sufficient room for vulva to fully open and release egg unless the adjacent body wall muscles are in a contracted state.
source: The functional purpose of this phase advance may be mechanical. Passage of each 25 × 40 µm egg requires contraction of vm1 and vm2 muscles on both the anterior and posterior sides of the vulva (Li et al., 2013). There may not be sufficient room for vulva to fully open and release egg unless the adjacent body wall muscles are in a contracted state.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation stated in the discussion.

claim: The HSNs are command neurons that integrate diverse sensory inputs and initiate the ~2 min active state of the egg-laying circuit.
source: The HSNs are command neurons that integrate diverse sensory inputs and initiate the ~2 min active state of the egg-laying circuit.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of HSN function.

claim: HSN makes and releases the neuromodulator serotonin which signals through G protein coupled serotonin receptors to activate the vulval muscles.
source: Instead, HSN makes and releases the neuromodulator serotonin which signals through G protein coupled serotonin receptors to activate the vulval muscles (Desai et al., 1988; Shyn et al., 2003; Carnell et al., 2005; Hobson et al., 2006; Hapiak et al., 2009).

claim: The HSNs also release serotonin onto the AVF interneurons in the nerve ring to promote a state of locomotion arousal that accompanies the active state.
source: The HSNs also release serotonin onto the AVF interneurons in the nerve ring to promote a state of locomotion arousal that accompanies the active state (Hardaker et al., 2001).

claim: Animals defective in serotonin signaling have reduced egg laying, but this defect is not as severe as that of egl-1(dm) animals missing HSNs.
source: Animals defective in serotonin signaling have reduced egg laying (Tanis et al., 2008), but this defect is not as severe as that of egl-1(dm) animals missing HSNs (Trent et al., 1983), suggesting HSN releases additional neurotransmitters.

claim: HSN releases additional neurotransmitters beyond serotonin.
source: Animals defective in serotonin signaling have reduced egg laying (Tanis et al., 2008), but this defect is not as severe as that of egl-1(dm) animals missing HSNs (Trent et al., 1983), suggesting HSN releases additional neurotransmitters.
evidence: This is inferred in the discussion from the comparison of serotonin-defective and HSN-deficient mutants.

claim: Optogenetic activation of HSNs leads to rhythmic activity of VC neurons, which are not known to express serotonin receptors.
source: We found that optogenetic activation of HSNs leads to rhythmic activity of VC neurons, which are not known to express serotonin receptors, so an unknown signal derived from HSN could directly activate VCs, as depicted in the Figure 7 model.

claim: An unknown signal derived from HSN could directly activate VCs.

claim: The HSNs receive little synaptic input near the vulval except from the PLM mechanosensory neurons.
source: The HSNs receive little synaptic input near the vulval except from the PLM mechanosensory neurons (White et al., 1986).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to previous anatomical work.

claim: The PLMs inhibit HSN activity and egg laying in response to gentle touch.
source: The PLMs inhibit HSN activity and egg laying in response to gentle touch (Zhang et al., 2008), but recent work indicates the PLM neurons are also deformed during normal patterns of locomotion that could contribute to rhythmic activity seen in HSN during egg laying (Topalidou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to previous work.

claim: The PLM neurons are deformed during normal patterns of locomotion that could contribute to rhythmic activity seen in HSN during egg laying.
source: The PLMs inhibit HSN activity and egg laying in response to gentle touch (Zhang et al., 2008), but recent work indicates the PLM neurons are also deformed during normal patterns of locomotion that could contribute to rhythmic activity seen in HSN during egg laying (Topalidou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to previous work.

claim: flp-10 and flp-17 neuropeptides are released from the CO2-responsive BAG neurons in the head, and these neuropeptides signal through EGL-6 receptor and Gαo to activate IRK channels that inhibit HSN activity and egg laying.

claim: There must be additional receptors and effectors of Gαo that inhibit HSN activity, because loss of EGL-6 or IRK channels do not increase egg laying as much as cell-specific inhibition of Gαo.
source: Because loss of EGL-6 or IRK channels do not increase egg laying as much as cell-specific inhibition of Gαo, there must be additional receptors and effectors of Gαo that inhibit HSN activity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an inference from genetic experiments.

claim: Gαq signaling opposes Gαo to increase serotonin release from the HSNs.
source: Gαq signaling opposes Gαo to increase serotonin release from the HSNs (Tanis et al., 2008), but the ligands and receptors that activate Gαq have not yet been identified.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to previous work.

claim: The ligands and receptors that activate Gαq in HSNs have not yet been identified.

claim: HSN Ca2+ transients vary more in frequency than amplitude.
source: Because we find that HSN Ca2+ transients vary more in frequency than amplitude, we propose that these diverse sensory signals increase or reduce the probability that HSN reaches a threshold potential that can initiate, sustain, or terminate HSN activity and thus the active behavior state of the egg-laying circuit.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on Ca2+ imaging observations.

claim: Diverse sensory signals increase or reduce the probability that HSN reaches a threshold potential that can initiate, sustain, or terminate HSN activity and thus the active behavior state of the egg-laying circuit.

evidence: This is a proposed model stated in the discussion.

claim: The accumulation of unlaid eggs in the uterus, perhaps leading to mechanical stretch, provides an essential, permissive signal for entry into the active state.
source: We propose that the accumulation of unlaid eggs in the uterus, perhaps leading to mechanical stretch, provides an essential, permissive signal for entry into the active state.

claim: Animals grown on food generate one new oocyte from each of two gonad arms every ~10 min.
source: Animals grown on food generate one new oocyte from each of two gonad arms every ~10 min, balancing out the 3–5 eggs laid in the ~2 min active state that occurs every ~20 min, to result in a ~constant number of unlaid eggs in the uterus (McCarter et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to previous work.

claim: Eight uterine muscles line the uterine lumen and form gap junctions with the vm2 muscles.
source: Eight uterine muscles line the uterine lumen and form gap junctions with the vm2 muscles (White et al., 1986), and the addition of unlaid eggs into the uterus could induce a mechanical stretch that cross-excites the vm2 muscles.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to previous anatomical work.

claim: The addition of unlaid eggs into the uterus could induce a mechanical stretch that cross-excites the vm2 muscles.

claim: Animal locomotion slows during egg release.
source: We found that animal locomotion slows during egg release, and that optogenetic activation of the VC neurons halts movement and results in body wall muscle contraction and animal shortening.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on data in Figure 3C.

claim: Optogenetic activation of the VC neurons halts movement and results in body wall muscle contraction and animal shortening.
source: We found that animal locomotion slows during egg release, and that optogenetic activation of the VC neurons halts movement and results in body wall muscle contraction and animal shortening.

claim: The effect of VC activity to slow locomotion and contract body wall muscles may help compress the body and uterus to encourage expulsion of eggs.
source: The effect of VC activity to slow locomotion and contract body wall muscles may help compress the body and uterus to encourage expulsion of eggs, analogous to the role of body wall muscle contraction in facilitating defecation (Liu and Thomas, 1994).
evidence: This is a proposed function stated in the discussion.

claim: The vulval muscles express nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
source: The vulval muscles also express nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, and receptor agonists including levamisole and nicotine stimulate egg laying (Weinshenker et al., 1995; Waggoner et al., 2000).

claim: Receptor agonists including levamisole and nicotine stimulate egg laying.
source: The vulval muscles also express nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, and receptor agonists including levamisole and nicotine stimulate egg laying (Weinshenker et al., 1995; Waggoner et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to previous work.

claim: Acetylcholine released from the VA/VB motor neurons signal through nicotinic receptors on the vm1 muscles to stimulate rhythmic vulval muscle twitching, which combined with acetylcholine released from the VC neurons to similarly excite the vm2 muscles results in egg laying.
source: These data together are consistent with a model in which acetylcholine released from the VA/VB motor neurons signal through nicotinic receptors on the vm1 muscles to stimulate rhythmic vulval muscle twitching, which combined with acetylcholine released from the VC neurons to similarly excite the vm2 muscles results in egg laying.

source: High levels of VC activity, such as occurs during optogenetic activation, may drive release of additional signals, such as neuropeptides, that inhibit egg-laying circuit activity (Bany et al., 2003; Banerjee and Francis, personal communication), or by freezing locomotion may feedback to halt the VA/VB activity required to drive vm1 contraction.

We found that inhibition of egg laying by exogenous tyramine is reduced but not eliminated in lgc-55 null mutants, suggesting other tyramine receptors help terminate the active state.
